Hi community,

I am facing a critical issue with App Proxy in my custom Shopify app (built with Laravel). The App Proxy always returns a 404 error, and the requests never reach my AWS server via the storefront.

However, after running several isolation tests, I found a conclusive result that points directly to Shopify’s internal routing infrastructure.

Here are the details of my setup and the exact test results:

[App Proxy Configuration]

Subpath prefix: apps

Subpath: my-app-subpath

Proxy URL: [https://sub.example.com/front](https://sub.example.com/front)

[The Problem] Whether a user is logged in or browsing as a guest, accessing the proxy URL via the storefront always results in a 404 error in the browser console: GET https://[my-shop-domain][.myshopify.com/apps/my-app-subpath](https://.myshopify.com/apps/my-app-subpath) net::ERR_BLOCKED_BY_RESPONSE 404 (Not Found) When this happens, absolutely no requests are recorded in my AWS ALB or Nginx access logs.

[Conclusive Test Result: Direct URL Access Works Perfectly] To isolate the issue, I modified the URL and tested a direct connection to my server, bypassing Shopify’s proxy:

Direct URL Tested: [https://sub.example.com/front/](https://sub.example.com/front/)[dummy_customer_id]

Result: It works perfectly! The page renders completely fine, and my Nginx logs immediately capture the request with a 200 OK.

This direct test completely rules out any firewall, AWS WAF, security group, or Nginx routing misconfigurations on my AWS side. My server is fully live, publicly accessible, and working flawlessly.

Additionally, I tested with another app variant whose App Proxy URL uses a CloudFlare tunnel — that worked perfectly. So Shopify IS able to reach a different URL on the same server infrastructure, which further confirms the issue is specific to how Shopify’s routing handles this particular app’s proxy configuration.

[Hypothesis & Question] The fact that the server is 100% reachable directly, but completely invisible (0 logs) when requested through https://[my-shop-domain][.myshopify.com/apps/my-app-subpath](https://.myshopify.com/apps/my-app-subpath), proves that Shopify’s proxy server is dropping the traffic internally before it even attempts to forward the packet to my Proxy URL.

(Note on history: The dev environment server was down/stopped for a few months until recently, and this issue might have even existed before the server went down. It seems like Shopify’s internal routing table or cache for this specific app has been heavily frozen or corrupted over this period.)

Is there any way to force-refresh or clear Shopify’s internal App Proxy routing cache for a specific app? Or can a Shopify engineer look into the internal routing state for this proxy setup to reset the handshake?

Any help would be greatly appreciated. Thank you!

What I particularly like about this approach is that you can start with a fairly straightforward points program and then build something considerably more sophisticated around it as the brand grows.

Mage Loyalty | Retention & Loyalty for Shopify brands

  Mage is a Retention & Loyalty platform built for Shopify brands. Build an advanced loyalty program that goes deeper than simple points & rewards.

2. Smile.io - a good option for straightforward Shopify loyalty programs

Smile is one of the better-known Shopify loyalty and rewards apps, and for good reason.

It’s particularly attractive if you want to get a traditional loyalty program up and running without overcomplicating things.

You can build programs around:

Points

Rewards

Referrals

VIP tiers

Customer engagement

Shopify POS

One of the things I’d consider with Smile is how much complexity you actually need. If you want a relatively conventional “earn points → redeem rewards → refer friends” loyalty program, it covers the fundamentals well.

It also has a long track record in the Shopify ecosystem, which can be important if you want something established and widely used.

I’d put Smile on the shortlist for small-to-medium Shopify stores that want a proven loyalty and rewards platform without needing a huge amount of customization.

3. Yotpo Loyalty & Referrals - good if you already use the Yotpo ecosystem

Yotpo is another major option, particularly for larger Shopify brands.

Its loyalty product covers the usual areas such as points, rewards, VIP tiers, referrals and customer engagement, and it has the advantage of sitting within the broader Yotpo ecosystem.

Simple loyalty program: Smile is worth looking at.

I’d also avoid choosing a loyalty app purely based on the number of features on the pricing page. The important question is whether you’ll actually use those features to change customer behaviour.

jwkdp’s point deserves more attention than it got, because it splits this whole app category in two. Most apps that put component SKUs into orders do it by editing the order after it is created. That works until something downstream reads the order first: a 3PL with instant order import, an ERP connector, a Flow trigger. A few things that actually decide whether a bundle app raises AOV or just causes support tickets:

Pick the bundle type from your catalog, not the app. Products people buy together anyway → fixed bundle. Lots of similar items (candles, snacks, socks) → mix & match / “any 3 for $X”. Check variants. If your products have sizes/colours, make sure “2 × same product, different variants” still counts as a bundle.

Look at it on mobile with your real theme. Most bundle traffic is mobile; a widget that pushes “Add to cart” below the fold costs you more than the bundle earns.

Measure AOV for bundle orders vs. non-bundle orders for a week before and after. If the app can’t show you that, Shopify’s reports can with a discount filter.

What happened: Marketplace Connect stopped accepting new Etsy connections in October 2025 and Etsy development on it is frozen. Existing connections still run, but it isn’t being maintained, so treat it as end-of-life rather than “working fine”. The trigger appears to have been Etsy making readiness_state_id mandatory on 30 September 2025 with short notice. Etsy ships breaking changes like that periodically, and an unmaintained integration breaks on the next one.

What’s actually available instead, honestly, including the annoying parts:

QuickSync: biggest install base, straightforward setup.

CedCommerce: most feature-complete and the most complex. Good support reputation, but expect real setup time.

LitCommerce: cleanest UI of the group, multi-channel if you sell beyond Etsy.

DPL: cheaper end, narrower feature set.

All roughly $9-99/month depending on order volume.

The thing I’d check before installing any of them: filter the reviews to 1 star and read the last six months. The failure mode in this category isn’t “sync is slow”, it’s the app writing something to your shop you never approved. Recurring examples across apps include prices being reset, price sync running while the setting was off, listing data being overwritten, and bulk listing duplication that costs real money in listing fees.

Two safeguards regardless of which you pick:

Turn off every sync direction you don’t specifically need, especially price. Verify it’s still off after any app update.

Test on 2-3 listings for a week before connecting your whole catalogue. Recovering an overwritten catalogue by hand is days of work.

Also worth knowing about the underlying API, because it explains a lot of the flakiness: Etsy has no webhooks for listing changes. Every app in this category is polling on a schedule, so anything advertising “real-time two-way sync” is describing a poll loop. That’s fine, but it means conflicts get resolved by whoever polled last, which is how “it changed my prices” happens without anyone doing anything malicious.

Full disclosure since it’s relevant: this problem is annoying enough that I’m building an alternative focused on it, sync that shows you a diff of every proposed change and writes nothing until you approve it. Full disclosure: I work at Printbox, we build web-to-print software, so factor that in. The thread is old and still unsolved, so this is partly for people arriving from search.

One correction on the framing first, because it changes what you should be shopping for. Your preset sizes are not a variant problem. Six sizes across four quantities is about two dozen variants, comfortably inside Shopify’s limits. What variants cannot do is hold a number the customer types in. The problem to solve is pricing a value that does not exist until the customer enters it, and then getting Shopify to actually charge that price.

Worth knowing about the two apps recommended above, and most option apps generally: they work by adding a surcharge to a base variant price. Pick this option, add two dollars. That handles your presets well. It gets awkward when the price has to be computed from dimensions the customer supplies, because there is no surcharge table to look the answer up in.

On modeling the pricing itself, this will save you maintaining a discount matrix by hand. Per unit price falls with quantity in print because a real chunk of the cost is fixed per job: setup, the cut, the material you waste at the start of a roll. If you price as setup plus (area times quantity times rate), the declining per unit curve comes out on its own, and it stays correct at custom sizes you never thought to put in a table. Hand built discount tiers give you numbers you have to revisit every time material costs move.

The thing to test before committing to any app: that the price shown in the widget is the price Shopify charges at checkout. Ask how it gets there. A hidden add-on line item, a draft order, or Shopify Functions with cart transform. Functions is the current clean answer. The other two work, but they leak, usually into discount codes and abandoned cart flows behaving strangely.

Doing all of it in one place (custom dimensions, area and quantity pricing, and a print ready file with the cut path already on it at the end) is what enterprise web-to-print covers, running white label under your own brand. It’s priced for shops where custom print is the whole business, so it’s a bigger step than an options app. Written up here: Sticker Design and Print-on-Demand Software | Printbox

Disclosure up front: we make a push notification app (PushEngage), so take this with that in mind. We’re not naming apps here on purpose, because the point applies to all of them.

Something we see a lot of store owners get caught out by: push and messaging apps bill on very different meters, and the cheapest-looking plan on the pricing page is often not the cheapest for your store.

The three common meters:

Per notification sent or delivered. Cheap if you send a weekly promo. Gets expensive once you turn on abandoned cart, back-in-stock and shipping updates, because those fire constantly and they’re the ones that actually make money.

Per subscriber, in tiers. You pay for everyone who opted in, whether they’re active or not. Sending more doesn’t raise the bill, but a big list of people who subscribed two years ago and never came back does. Check whether the app lets you remove inactive subscribers, and whether that lowers your tier.

Per monthly active user (mostly for stores with a mobile app). You pay for devices that opened the app in the last 30 days, so your bill goes up exactly when engagement goes up.

Before installing anything, pull three numbers:

how many subscribers you’d start with (or expect after 3 months)

roughly what share of them are active in a month

how many notifications each subscriber would get in a month once your automations are on, not just your campaigns

Then work out the monthly bill on each app’s meter with those numbers. It takes about 10 minutes in a spreadsheet, and it usually changes which app looks cheapest.

Happy to help anyone run the numbers for their store in the replies. Just share rough figures, no store names needed.

Hiring a model, booking a studio, and shooting each piece costs serious time and money — and that’s before retouching.

I used to do the thing most of us do: upload the supplier’s plain white-background shots and hope for the best. They’re clean, but they don’t tell a story. A t-shirt on a hanger doesn’t look like a t-shirt someone would wear.

So over the past few months I’ve been testing a completely different workflow: AI-generated product photography — replacing models, backgrounds, and scenes in bulk, without a single photoshoot. Here’s exactly how it works, the good and the not-so-good.

The workflow

Step 1 — Start with clean product shots

You don’t need fancy photos. Plain shots of the product on a white or neutral background work best — supplier images, or even photos taken on your phone.

Step 2 — Pick your products in bulk

Instead of editing images one by one, I select products by category or tag — for example, “all hoodies from the fall collection.” The tool only touches exactly what I want.

Step 3 — Choose a model & scene

This is the fun part. You pick an AI model (a professional-looking man or woman), a scene (studio, street, urban), and any persona you want to keep consistent. Once you save them, you can reuse the same model + scene across your whole catalog — which is what makes your store look like it has one cohesive brand, not 50 random photos.

Step 4 — Generate, compare, save

Each image generates in under a minute. You see a side-by-side preview of the original vs. the result before saving, so nothing gets accidentally overwritten. Then save directly to the product — either replace the existing image or keep it as an extra photo.

Speed: I processed a whole season’s worth of products in one afternoon.

Consistency: Same model, same scene, same lighting across every product = a store that finally looks professional.

Cost: A fraction of one studio shoot. (This is the part that shocked me — a full shoot for 50 SKUs would’ve been thousands of dollars.)

What to watch out for

AI is great, but check the details — hands, logos, and text can sometimes look odd. Always preview before saving.

Don’t use it for everything. Hero images on your homepage benefit from real photography. Batch AI editing shines for catalog/product pages and new-season launches.

Disclosure first: I build EZStock, so read this as a developer answering your spec, not a neutral recommendation. Going through your points in order, including where the tradeoff sits.

Variant-level thresholds, no tagging: yes. Reorder points are set per variant, not per product, and low stock is judged per variant against that point. Nothing lives on tags, so there’s nothing to maintain on the product records.

Email alerts with a report: yes. It’s an opt-in daily digest, one email listing everything at or below its reorder point, and it only sends when that list actually changes so you’re not getting the same “still low” mail every morning. The full list rides along as a CSV attachment with a suggested order quantity per line, so you can open it in a spreadsheet or forward it to a supplier without logging in.

Red/yellow/green dashboard: yes. The home screen shows three counts across everything you track: order-now (out or at/below reorder), running-low (approaching it), and healthy (well above). Same red/amber/green split you’re used to.

Excluding variants: yes. There’s a per-variant “exclude from alerts” toggle for the end-of-line, made-to-order, and bundle items you don’t restock, so they stop showing up in the digest without you deleting the product.

Forecasting: yes, and this is where it separates from the lighter tools in this thread. It computes demand from your actual sales history and does ABC grading, not just days-of-cover arithmetic. If real forecasting is a requirement rather than a nice-to-have, that’s the piece most of the low-stock apps here skip.

Cost: there’s a free plan, and the forecasting/ABC/reporting tier is $49/month, which lands in the range you gave.

Your Venture 8.0.0 theme doesn’t matter here either way. Inventory apps run in the admin, not on your storefront, so an old or unsupported theme has no bearing on this category. You can cross that worry off.

One honest caveat to weigh against Merchbees: EZStock doesn’t have a long review history yet. Happy to help you run it against a real PO or your actual catalog if you want to see whether it holds up before you commit.

@JohnSmith2, one point I don’t think anyone has covered yet: you said the goal is enough stock to keep production flowing. That changes the alert you actually need.

A fixed low-stock threshold per variant (“alert me at 20”) fires at the same level in your slow month and your peak month. So it’s either too late in peak season or too noisy in the off-season. For production planning, the more useful trigger is days of cover against lead time. For example: “This variant has 18 days of stock left at the current sales rate, and production or your supplier needs 21. Act now.” The threshold then moves with your sales on its own, with no re-tuning every season.

Against your list:

Variant-level, no tags, and exclusions: any decent tool should let you pick variants directly.

Emailed CSV: check that it shows why each variant is flagged (days left versus lead time), not just the stock count.

Red/yellow/green: worth defining as red = days left is under lead time, yellow = under lead time plus a safety buffer, green = fine.

Forecasting: the minimum to look for is seasonality from at least 12 months of sales. Otherwise it just averages last month.

Disclosure: I build custom inventory dashboards, so I’m biased. I have a demo that does the days-of-cover approach, with a forecast per item, reorder-by dates and a red/yellow/green status, and I’m happy to show it if useful. If none of the off-the-shelf apps fit your exact spec, I do this as a small fixed-price build. Happy to talk by DM. Otherwise, I hope the framing above helps you test whichever app you trial.

The main thing worth deciding before you pick one is where the registry actually lives, because it splits the options in half.

Off-site platforms like MyRegistry host the list on their own domain and let the couple add items from any store. Great reach, but the traffic and the shopper data land there rather than with you, and the gift usually arrives as a plain order you cannot connect back to the registry.

On-site apps keep the registry on your own store as a real page. The registrant shares your URL, guests land on your catalogue, and their purchases attribute back to the registry so you can see which events are actually producing revenue.

Whichever way you go, check these three things, because they are where most registry apps quietly fall down:

Does the gift ship to the registrant’s address automatically, or does the guest have to type it in and hope? This is the one shoppers notice.

Does an item mark itself as purchased when the order comes in, including partial quantities, so two guests do not buy the same thing?

Does it survive a theme change? Registry apps that inject into theme markup break the moment you switch themes.

Swym is the most established on-site option. MyRegistry is worth a look if cross-store reach matters more to you than owning the traffic.

Disclosure: I build Listify, another on-site registry app, so take my framing with that in mind. It covers the three points above and has a free plan if you want to see the shopper flow before committing.
